hints: Notice the thermistor is connected directly across the cell with negligible internal resistance, so the p.d. $V$ across it stays equal to the e.m.f.
Recall how the resistance of an NTC thermistor changes when temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ increases.
Use $P = V^2/R$ with constant $V$ to decide whether $P$ rises or falls when $R$ falls, and whether the change is linear.
walkthrough: The circuit is a single loop with the thermistor across the cell. With negligible internal resistance, the p.d. across the thermistor $V$ equals the cell e.m.f. and stays constant.
For the usual NTC thermistor, resistance $R$ decreases as temperature increases.
Power dissipated can be written with constant $V$ as $P = V^2/R$.
As temperature rises, $R$ gets smaller, so the fraction $V^2/R$ gets larger. Hence $P$ increases with temperature.

Because $P$ varies as $1/R$ and $R$ itself varies non-linearly with temperature, the $P$-temperature graph curves upward from a small positive value rather than being straight or flat. This is option A.

options.A: Resistance of the NTC thermistor falls with temperature, so with constant $V$, $P = V^2/R$ increases with an upward curve.
options.B: A falling $P$ against temperature would need resistance to increase with temperature, which is opposite to NTC thermistor behaviour.
options.C: Constant $P$ would need constant resistance, but thermistor resistance changes significantly with temperature.
options.D: A straight-line fall to zero does not match $P = V^2/R$ with decreasing $R$, which gives a rising non-linear curve.
